why: THIS FILE IS NOT PART OF THE BEHAVIOR CORPUS. Every `outcome` below is a fact about behavior-run.js -- about the INSTRUMENT -- and not about any WebAPI member, which is why it may be written here by hand: nothing in it judges an implementation. It lives outside tests/fixtures/behavior-cases/ so it can never be loaded as a case, and no entry asks a question whose answer differs between engines.
what: The runner is evaluated by four callers, two of which (tests/quality.rs inside Korvus, plugins/korvus-persona/capture/oracle.mjs inside a real Chrome over CDP) have their answers compared to each other case by case. If those two ever evaluate under different rules, a harness difference becomes a recorded behavior difference and the corpus is silently wrong. Both sides run THIS file and must produce THIS map: `cargo test -p korvus-webapi --test behavior_runner_async` and `node plugins/korvus-persona/capture/oracle.mjs --selftest`.

note: Listed BEFORE the synchronous case that sets the global, and still sees its value: proof that awaited cases run in a second pass after every synchronous case, which is what keeps capture/collect.js's single-task guarantee intact for the synchronous corpus.
`undefined` is its own outcome, never `unsupported` -- every void method returns it.

THE REGRESSION GUARD FOR THE WHOLE CHANGE. Without `await: true` a promise is still an object the transport cannot carry, exactly as before. If this ever answers `{value:1}` the flip went global and every one of the ~137 members recorded as "[object Promise]" has been silently re-answered.
The one question the synchronous runner could ask of a promise-returning member. It must keep working, because ~137 recorded cases are exactly this.
The flag never creates a deadline timer for a value that is not thenable.
null is a value; undefined is not. The corpus distinguishes them and so must this.
Settling does not widen the carrier: an object is still unrecordable, so an awaited member with no scalar surface is asked for its brand instead.
The awaited path shares `jsonSafe`, so the value that once killed a chunk of thirty cases costs one case here too.
await routes a rejection into the same catch the synchronous path already had, which is why `wakeLock.request("screen")` can be recorded as `throws: NotAllowedError` for free.
Marked awaitable but never reaching a promise at all: still a throw, not a timeout.
50 ms against a 1500 ms deadline. Also proves the caller is really pumping timers: on the Korvus side a runtime that only drained microtasks would report a timeout here.

THE HONESTY REQUIREMENT. A question that never settles is reported as a timeout and nothing else -- not `undefined` (which is a real answer a member can give), not `unsupported` (which says the transport was too narrow). `outcomeToCase` drops it rather than recording it, and the Korvus side prints the member name.
